note: Each entry is a release that fixed something Docket got wrong. 'release' is a public GitHub release of this site's repo and 'date' is the day it was published (UTC). 'tests' are files in Docket's tests/ folder that fail on the code from before the fix. scripts/verify_corrections.py checks the release, the date and the tests against GitHub and the app repo on every deploy. Newest first. Written from docs/IMPROVEMENT_LOG.md in the app repo; nothing here is added unless the log or a commit says it.

entries.title: The command line scored a mistyped address as a site, and the free version quoted the wrong price
entries.wrong: docket audit "not a url" crawled nothing, scored the address 0 with every area "not applicable" and exited 0, so a typo in a deploy script looked like a passing run. Without a key, the command line's footer quoted $59 once or 4 x $14.75 all through the Black Friday sale, while the app quoted $29.50. Licence messages said "This Mac" on Windows too.
entries.found: An independent full audit of the product and this site, ordered by the owner, ran the command line with a malformed address and read its footer against the live offer.
entries.fixed: An address with a space, a malformed port or no host is refused before any crawl, with exit code 1. The free footer reads the same live offer as the app and gives the sale price while the sale runs. Licence messages say "computer": one licence covers up to 3 computers at a time, Mac or Windows.

entries.title: The free command line always reported success, and a free diff said nothing had changed
entries.wrong: Without a key, docket audit exited 0 on every site, including one whose homepage told search engines not to index it and one that did not answer at all, so a deploy gate built on the free command line could never fail. Comparing a clean site with one carrying dozens of planted problems, a free docket diff printed "No change in findings between the two." and passed.
entries.found: An independent full audit of the product and this site, ordered by the owner, ran the free command line against local test sites and checked the exit code of each run.
entries.fixed: The free command line now exits 2 at the --fail-on threshold, as the paid one does, and says the threshold was reached. A free diff says how many problems got worse and how many got better, and fails the build on the real regressions; which ones they are is in the paid version.

entries.title: Reports listed an audit Docket could not judge with an ordinary score
entries.wrong: When Docket could not read enough of a site to judge it, the report itself said to treat the score as unknown, but the Reports list showed the kept audit with a plain number beside every other audit. Every kept report was also stored with no grade.
entries.found: Building the tools that let an AI assistant read kept audits: the list was fed the score without the two facts that say whether it is a verdict on the site.
entries.fixed: A kept audit now keeps its grade and whether its score speaks for the site, and the Reports list marks it the way the results screen does. Audits kept before this keep their old row.

entries.title: A site with no business markup scored 100 for AI search visibility
entries.wrong: A six-page property manager's site with no structured data at all scored 100 for AI search visibility, in a report whose own text said structured data is where the gains in AI answers come from. A site that had added business markup but no profile links lost points in the same area, so doing less scored better. The same audit gave Structured data 77 with no structured data on any page.
entries.found: The owner of the report asked how AI visibility could be 100 with no structured data. A bare test site then showed the same shape in four more areas: Social and sharing 94 with no Open Graph tags, Tracking 72.5 with no analytics, and Security 58 with no HTTPS.
entries.fixed: No business markup now costs the AI area as well, as the same job as the Structured data finding. An area whose whole subject is missing holds at 45, in the red, wherever Docket can be sure of the absence.

entries.title: The app quoted the old price after Docket became $59
entries.wrong: Docket's price fell from $349 to $59 on 2 November. Every copy up to 1.3.138 holds the list price it was built with, and trusts the price the website publishes only when the two agree, so it went on showing $349, or four payments of $87.25, beside the Buy button. The checkout charged the new price.
entries.found: The price change itself: the website moved to $59 the same day, and the app's own still of a free audit still printed $349.
entries.fixed: The app now states $59, or four payments of $14.75. A price under the checkout's $50.01 minimum for paying in four, such as the $29.50 Black Friday price, is shown with no instalments, even if the website's offer file carries one. The sale is shown under the name the website gives it, with no limit on buyers.

entries.title: A large site that asks crawlers to wait could not be audited whole in a day
entries.wrong: Docket waits the delay a site's robots.txt asks for between requests. A furniture retailer with about 23,000 pages asking for 4 seconds would have taken about 26 hours, longer than the day an audit may run, so even its owner could not audit the whole site.
entries.found: A whole-site audit of a large furniture retailer, with its robots.txt asking for a 4-second wait, stopped long before the end.
entries.fixed: An owner auditing their own site can now choose not to wait the delay. Every page robots.txt blocks is still left unread, and the report says the delay was skipped and that Google does not read it at all. By default the delay is kept, as before.

entries.title: A gym marked up as a gym was told it had no local business markup
entries.wrong: A CrossFit gym whose homepage marks it up with schema.org's ExerciseGym type, address and phone included, was told at high severity that it had no local business markup. Docket recognised a hand-picked list of local business types that left out ExerciseGym and most others. Once the gym was recognised, the same homepage's shorter of two descriptions was checked instead of its full one, and fields the page does publish were called missing. Separately, a food bank's phone links with an extension written as a letter and digits were described as numbers spelled in letters that dial nothing.
entries.found: False-positive hunts on a CrossFit gym's site and a food bank's site, with every finding read against the live pages and the list of types read from schema.org's own vocabulary.
entries.fixed: Docket now recognises every local business type in schema.org's vocabulary, less public services and broadcasters, and checks the most complete of a site's own descriptions. A phone link with an extension is described as an extension, with the standard way to write one; a number really spelled in letters keeps its finding.

entries.title: One address was reported as 18 variations, by a fix two releases earlier
entries.wrong: The 1.3.134 change that reads a US address line however it is capitalised started the line at the first number it could find. On a florist whose shop pages show a result count just before the address, a different count on every page, that count was read as part of the address, and one address was reported as 18 address variations.
entries.found: A false-positive hunt on a florist's site the day after 1.3.134 shipped, reading each variation against the page it came from.
entries.fixed: The address line now starts at the last number that can begin a street line, and a number after Suite, Ste, Apt or # stays inside the address rather than starting it. The accounting firm whose address prompted 1.3.134 is still read correctly.

entries.title: A winery's reviews page was not counted as showing reviews
entries.wrong: A family winery whose reviews page shows quoted reviews signed by its customers was told at medium severity that it had no customer reviews or testimonials on the pages checked, that page among them. An auto repair shop built on Kukui, a website platform for repair shops, showed no platform at all.
entries.found: False-positive hunts on a family winery's site and an auto repair shop's site, with every finding read against the live pages.
entries.fixed: A page named Reviews or Testimonials by its address or its main heading now counts as labelled, and it still has to show a quoted review, a star rating or two signed reviews; a reviews page with nothing on it, and quotes on a page about something else, still do not count. Kukui is recognised from the address its files load from.

entries.title: An accounting firm was told it was not a local business, and an inn that its titles named no place
entries.wrong: An accounting firm whose header gives its full street address, with the town in capital letters, on every page was told it did not look like a local business, so none of the local checks ran for an office its clients visit. A country inn whose every page title names its state, the state of its own address, was told at medium severity that no page title mentioned a location.
entries.found: False-positive hunts on an accounting firm's site and a country inn's site, with every finding read against the live pages.
entries.fixed: A whole US address line ending in a town, a two-letter state code and a ZIP code now counts as an address however it is capitalised, both for deciding that the local checks apply and in the address check itself, without counting one address twice. The state of a site's own address, written as a code before its ZIP or in its markup, now counts as a location in its titles. A town and ZIP with no street, a year and a mailing address still do not count as a place to visit.

entries.title: A law firm was told it had no map, stray typefaces and no recognised profiles
entries.wrong: A family-law firm's site was told it had no map, though its directions page embeds a Google map that loads as the visitor scrolls. It was told none of its typefaces was used site-wide and that the rest pointed to an old template or an embedded widget, when Docket had read the stylesheets of only a few of its pages; Font Awesome was counted as one of the typefaces. Its structured data links its Martindale, Avvo and Lawyers.com profiles, and it was told it linked none Docket recognised.
entries.found: A false-positive hunt on a family-law firm's site, with each finding read against the live pages and the site's stylesheets measured by hand.
entries.fixed: A frame whose address waits in a lazy-loading attribute is read the way lazy images already were. Pages whose stylesheets were left unread by Docket's size limit are no longer counted, and the finding says how many were left out. Font Awesome is recognised as an icon font under its hyphenated name. Martindale, Avvo and Lawyers.com count as recognised profiles, and a site with none is no longer told it has only zero.

entries.title: Two builder-made sites were told they lacked a postcode, a map and proof they showed, and named the wrong platform
entries.wrong: An electrician's site with its full address and postcode in the footer of every page was told no postcode appeared anywhere and to put one in the footer; its contact page map, a builder's map widget, was reported as no map; and its typeface count included three stand-in fonts that are Arial sized to match the real ones. A plumber's homepage saying it is licensed and insured and recognised by the state board that licenses it was told it showed no certifications. Duda sites showed no platform, and GoDaddy sites would have shown the name of a GoDaddy subsidiary on the report cover.
entries.found: False-positive hunts on a plumber's GoDaddy site and an electrician's Duda site, with every finding read against the live pages, and the homepages of four Duda sites and several GoDaddy sites from public lists.
entries.fixed: The postcode check now reads the footer, as Docket's other address checks already did. An element named as a map that holds a latitude and a longitude counts as a map. Licence phrases such as licensed and insured count as proof; the word licensed alone does not. A font face whose only source is a font already on the computer is not counted as a typeface. Duda is recognised from its own markup, and GoDaddy's builder is named GoDaddy.

entries.title: Four corrections from two sites: a robots.txt the owner cannot edit, the wrong platform, reviews not seen, and the wrong cause for broken markup
entries.wrong: On a Squarespace site, a finding about AI crawler names their makers no longer use gave a block to paste into robots.txt; Squarespace's own help says its users cannot access or edit that file, and the lines come from Squarespace's setting for blocking AI crawlers. A site built with Webflow was reported as running on WordPress, because its structured data, pasted from a template, pointed at a WordPress-style image folder; a second Webflow site showed no platform at all. The same Webflow site's homepage shows 24 Google reviews under a line counting more than two thousand, and was told at medium severity that it had no customer reviews. Its high-severity structured-data finding said three blocks each held two separate JSON documents; each held one document followed by three closing brackets that closed nothing.
entries.found: False-positive hunts on a photographer's Squarespace portfolio and a dental practice's Webflow site, with every finding read against the live pages, Squarespace's help pages on robots.txt and on asking AI models to exclude a site, and the homepages of three real Webflow sites.
entries.fixed: On Squarespace the robots.txt finding still lists the retired names, and its fix now names the setting and links Squarespace's help page instead of offering markup. Docket now reads Webflow's own markup first, and text inside structured data no longer decides the platform. Two or more different first-name-and-initial names near a reviews label now count as reviews, as two dash signatures already did; one such name, or names with no reviews label, still do not. When what is left after a complete block starts with a closing bracket, the finding says the block closes more brackets than it opens and gives the line where the leftover starts; two documents in one block keep the two-documents advice.

entries.title: Docket said Google slows down for a site's crawl-delay rule; Google ignores it
entries.wrong: When an audit ran out of time on a site whose robots.txt asks for a delay between requests, the report said such a site is read slowly by every crawler, Google included. Google's robots.txt documentation lists crawl-delay among the rules it does not support.
entries.found: A whole-site audit of a large furniture retailer that stopped at the 15-minute limit, read against Google's own documentation.
entries.fixed: The report now says that crawlers which honour the rule, Docket among them, read such a site slowly, and that Google does not read it at all. Choosing Everything now allows an audit up to a day, and Finish now keeps the pages already read.

entries.title: A Squarespace site was told nothing about its visitors was being recorded
entries.wrong: A photographer's portfolio on Squarespace had no third-party analytics tag, and Docket said at high priority that nothing about visitor numbers, traffic sources, or which pages generate enquiries was being recorded. Squarespace's own Traffic panel counts unique visitors, visits and pageviews on every plan, without a tag.
entries.found: A false-positive hunt on a Squarespace portfolio, reading each finding against the live site and Squarespace's own help article.
entries.fixed: On Squarespace, as already on Wix, the absence of a third-party tag is stated as a notice that says the platform records visits itself, and what a third-party tag adds.

entries.title: Structured data naming a business after its template's own tag was not reported
entries.wrong: When a page's template failed to fill a value inside quotes, such as the business name, the structured data was still valid JSON, so Docket said nothing while the markup told every reader the business was called something like {{ studio.name }}.
entries.found: Working through the list of gaps a paying user would notice first, rebuilt from two weeks of audits of real sites.
entries.fixed: A value that is wholly a template tag, or a field that names or locates the business holding one, is reported with the field and the tag. A tag inside running text, such as a code example in an article, is not.

entries.title: One broken structured-data mistake was reported as two, with advice that pointed elsewhere
entries.wrong: When the same JSON-LD mistake appeared on several pages at different places, such as a trailing comma, the report counted it as different kinds of error and said fixing one would not make the pages valid, although one fix covered them all; it then offered a general list of possible causes instead of the specific one. When a page's template printed its own tag into the structured data instead of a value, the report quoted the parser's message and suggested looking for a trailing comma.
entries.found: Rebuilding the list of gaps a paying user would notice first from two weeks of audits of real sites, and measuring the structured-data finding against test pages.
entries.fixed: Errors are grouped by cause rather than by where they occur, so the specific fix is given. When the parse fails inside an unfilled template tag, the finding names the tag and its line and says to fix the template.

entries.title: A theme's menu icon and its code-block fonts were counted as brand typefaces
entries.wrong: The brand check told the same property manager its site used 11 different typefaces, 10 of them site-wide, and that each was a font file visitors download. Three were not typefaces a brand chose: the theme's icon font, whose only use is drawing the menu button, and two system fonts the theme sets for code blocks, which are already on the visitor's computer. A run an hour earlier had said 8 site-wide.
entries.found: Fact-checking a second copy of the same client report, reading the site's own stylesheets.
entries.fixed: A font every use of which draws an icon glyph is recognised as an icon font, whatever it is called, and the system fonts used for code are left out like other system fonts. A monospace web font a brand does choose still counts. The same site now reads 8 typefaces, all web fonts its pages load.

entries.title: A property manager was offered video-game topics because of a word in its name
entries.wrong: With no topic typed, Docket works out what a site is about from its pages. On a property-management firm whose pages had nothing in common but the firm's name, it took a word from the name as the subject and suggested a dozen articles about video games. In the same report, five empty pages were described as a response a rate limiter or bot filter might hand out, an insecure embedded frame was called scripts or styles, and the first finding listed a blocked crawler among the possible causes when the pages were failing with server errors.
entries.found: Fact-checking a real report against the live site, page by page, before it went to a client.
entries.fixed: A word now counts as a site's subject only if the site uses it in its own words, not just inside its name; when nothing qualifies, Docket says so. Empty pages that each carry their own title are judged as the site's pages. The insecure-content finding names what it found and quotes one. When most of what could not be read came back as server errors, the first finding names them as the cause.

entries.title: A vet's homepage with an appointment link and a phone link was told it asked visitors to do nothing
entries.wrong: A veterinary hospital's homepage carries "Request an Appointment" and a tap-to-call "Call Us" link near the top. Docket said, at high severity, that no button or link on it asked the visitor to do anything, and, also at high severity, that the homepage did not state what the business does, because the first main heading held only the logo.
entries.found: Auditing three local businesses from source (a landscaper, a plumber and a veterinary hospital) and reading every finding against the page.
entries.fixed: Docket now reads "request an", "book an", "make an appointment" and "call us" as actions, counts any phone or text link as one, and takes the first main heading with words in it as the headline. The same release stops telling Wix sites that nothing about their visitors is recorded, since Wix records visits itself, and stops counting an image's file name in a logo's alt text as a second spelling of the business name.

entries.title: An online job board was treated as a local business because of its mailing address
entries.wrong: A job board's contact page gives a mailing address, under a line about liking post, and nothing else local: no phone number, no opening hours, no local business markup. Docket treated the site as a local business on that address alone, reported at high severity that it had no local business markup and no phone number, and added three more local findings about a storefront that does not exist.
entries.found: Auditing a job board from source and reading every finding against the page.
entries.fixed: An address labelled as being for post (mailing, postal, registered, billing or correspondence) no longer makes a site local on its own; a street address people are invited to visit still does. The same release stops calling an http:// link broken when a browser would reach it over https, and stops saying pages with Twitter/X tags have no card markup when only the card type is missing.

entries.title: A dental practice showing dozens of patient reviews was told it had none
entries.wrong: A dental practice's reviews page shows dozens of patient reviews, each signed "- Name" with an ordinary hyphen. Docket said the site had no customer reviews or testimonials on the pages it checked, the reviews page among them, and told the practice to add a testimonials section.
entries.found: Auditing a dental practice's site from source and reading every finding against the page.
entries.fixed: Docket recognised a signature only after a long dash, and the first signature sat further below the reviews heading than it looked. A hyphen now signs a review after the end of a sentence, never before a day or "Noon", and a run of signed reviews below a reviews heading counts. The same release stops auditing a sitemap plugin's browser view of the sitemap as a page, and stops calling a short notice with two links out a category listing.

entries.title: A page was called a layout-shift risk because of a logo on every page
entries.wrong: A site's logo, with no declared size, sat in its header and again in its footer on every page. On a page whose one picture had its size declared, that made two unsized images out of three, and Docket said the page was at high risk of layout shift. Measured in a browser, nothing on the page moved. Image-heavy pages with the same logo were not flagged, so the verdict tracked how few pictures a page had.
entries.found: Auditing a law firm's site from source, reading every finding against the page, and measuring the layout shift of the flagged pages in a browser.
entries.fixed: A picture that appears on most pages is read as part of the site's template, and a page is called high risk only when one of its own pictures has no size. A page whose own picture is unsized is still reported. The same release fixes two wrong findings from a blog audit: a theme's site-name heading was compared with a contact page's title instead of the page's own heading, and an avatar beside the author's reply in the comments was taken for the logo. It also starts asking servers for the homepage as Meta's search crawler, so a firewall refusing it is no longer reported as clean.

entries.title: A robots.txt block was said to stop AI assistants fetching a page a user asked about
entries.wrong: Docket's crawler list, and the AI crawler checker and the AI crawler directives article on this site, said that blocking ChatGPT-User, Perplexity-User or Meta-ExternalFetcher in robots.txt stops that assistant fetching your page when someone asks about it. The operators say otherwise: OpenAI says robots.txt rules may not apply to requests a user starts, Perplexity says its user fetcher generally ignores them, and Meta says its fetcher may bypass them. No audit finding printed the sentence, but the list shipped in every copy of Docket and these pages showed it.
entries.found: Re-reading each operator's own crawler documentation after the sources behind Docket's knowledge feed changed, then checking whether the app said the same as the feed.
entries.fixed: The list, the knowledge feed and both pages now say what each operator says. Claude-User is still described as stopped by a robots.txt block, because Anthropic says it is. The same release adds Meta-WebIndexer, Meta AI's search crawler, to the crawlers Docket checks, and stops the competitor comparison calling a site that blocks Google-Extended absent from AI answers: Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode follow the Googlebot rules.

entries.title: Structured data in an old CDATA wrapper was said to be thrown away by search engines
entries.wrong: Some sites still write their structured data inside an XHTML-era CDATA comment. Docket reported a complete block written that way at high severity, as data that search engines discard entirely. It is not valid JSON as written, but we could not find a source showing what search engines do with it, so the claim went further than we could support.
entries.found: Auditing an art museum's site from source and reading every finding against the page, then looking for a source for the claim and finding none that tests this wrapper.
entries.fixed: Docket now reads the block, and reports the wrapper at medium severity in words we can stand behind: it is not valid JSON as written, some parsers strip it, others may discard the block, and removing the wrapper makes it safe everywhere. Structured data broken in other ways is still high. The same release fixes two other wrong findings: parts of one serialised essay were called rival pages, and a Download link to an audio file was called vague anchor text.

entries.title: A page written in two languages was reported as a mislabelled translation
entries.wrong: Docket compares the language a page declares with the language its text reads as. An English page that lists events in Spanish, with English headings and English description, was reported as reading as Spanish under an English label, and described as a translation competing with its original for the wrong readers.
entries.found: Auditing a public library's site from source and reading every finding against the page. English carried about three fifths as much of the page's text as Spanish did; a real translation carries none of its original language.
entries.fixed: When the declared language carries a good share of the page as well, Docket treats the page as bilingual and says nothing. A translation labelled as its original is still reported. The same release corrects two other findings: a phone link written as a row of X's is called a placeholder rather than a vanity number, and a sitemap entry with the site's address written twice is named for what it is.

entries.title: Icon links named by the heading beside them were reported as having no text
entries.wrong: Accessible sites often build a card as an icon link that takes its name from the card's heading, with aria-labelledby. A screen reader announces the heading as the link's name. Docket did not read that attribute, so it counted every such link as having no anchor text at all, and told the site to add text that was already there.
entries.found: Auditing a city government's site from source and reading every finding against the page. On one page, all eighteen links Docket counted as empty were icon links named by the heading beside them.
entries.fixed: Docket now reads a link's name from aria-labelledby first, the way a screen reader does. A link that points at nothing still counts as empty. The same release fixes two other wrong findings: a favicon check the site refused was reported as a missing favicon, and one dropdown repeated once per location was counted as many form fields.

entries.title: Template text a page hides from everyone was reported as live and unfinished
entries.wrong: Page builders can leave unused template blocks in a page, with words like Lorem ipsum and Heading 2 text goes here, and switch them off in the page's own stylesheet so that no visitor ever sees them. Docket read the words in the HTML and reported, at high severity, that unfinished content was live and indexable, with advice to replace it or take the page out of search.
entries.found: Auditing a charity's site from source and reading every finding against the page. In a browser every one of the blocks was switched off and took up no space.
entries.fixed: Text the page hides from every visitor, with the hidden attribute, an inline style or a rule in its own stylesheet that applies at every screen size, is no longer read as placeholder text. The same words where a visitor can see them, including a block shown only on phones, are still reported. The same release fixes two other wrong findings: a docs site's section label read as a second brand name, and the weights of one font counted as separate typefaces.

entries.title: A link whose server hung up on Docket was reported as broken
entries.wrong: Docket checks a sample of the links a site makes to other sites. Some servers accept the connection and then close it without answering when the request comes from an audit tool, while a browser gets the page. Docket recorded that the same way as a server it could not reach at all, and told the site that working links were broken and should be updated or removed.
entries.found: Auditing a travel blog from source and reading every finding against the page. Both of its broken links opened in a browser, and the same request carrying Docket's name got no answer at all.
entries.fixed: Docket now tells a server that hung up from one it could not reach. A hang-up is listed with the links that refused an automated request, as links Docket could not check, and a link whose server cannot be reached at all is still reported as broken. The same release fixes two other wrong findings: a page quoting the words coming soon was read as unfinished, and a page whose two H1s say the same thing was counted as having more than one.

entries.title: A Cloudflare site's bot check was reported as AI crawlers refused
entries.wrong: Docket asks a site's server for the homepage as each AI crawler, from the user's own computer. Cloudflare checks real crawlers by the network address they come from, so to Cloudflare those requests are crawlers pretending, and it may challenge or turn them away while serving the real crawlers normally. Docket reported that as AI crawlers refused by the server, on two sites at critical severity and with a warning that search was blocked too, although the real crawlers read both. A server that asked a crawler to pay, with HTTP 402, was counted as having served the page.
entries.found: Before any ad said sites were blocking AI crawlers, we tested the check on twenty sites behind Cloudflare and compared each verdict with what each crawler is really served. Three sites block AI crawlers by name, and Docket was right about them; two were false blocks.
entries.fixed: When Cloudflare challenges the request, or refuses Docket's Googlebot request as well, Docket now says it could not test those crawlers from here, and where the real answer is: Cloudflare's security events, and Search Console for Google. A rule that refuses AI crawlers by name while Googlebot is served is still reported as a block. A 402 is reported as a request to pay, never as a page served. The same release fixes 24 other wrong findings, found by auditing real sites of several kinds and reading every finding against the page.

entries.title: The installed app kept no record of what its helpers did
entries.wrong: The desktop app starts Docket's engine with its output going nowhere. If the helper that renders pages in a browser was missing or broken, nothing said so: rendering was skipped, the checks that need it reported that they could not confirm, and the report looked like an audit where rendering had simply found nothing. Starting the installed engine with an empty home folder left no log at all.
entries.found: Another of our apps found a doubling in speed by reading its log. Docket had no log to read, so a support question would have been answered from the customer's description of it.
entries.fixed: The engine now writes a log file in the .docket folder in your home folder: the version, the licence mode (never the key), and for the render helper whether it was found, where, and whether it runs. It adds a line for each audit that names the host and nothing more. The file stays on your Mac and nothing sends it. The build now starts the finished app with an empty home folder and refuses to ship unless the log says the render helper runs. It then points the engine at a file that cannot run and requires the log to say so.

entries.title: Five wrong findings, found by auditing our own sites
entries.wrong: Docket read a date followed by a sentence ("last updated 2026-09-15 The fastest way:") as the street address "15 The fastest way". That made a Mac app a local business, and its two top findings were high severity: no phone number and no LocalBusiness markup. It read a licence date followed by a year range as a phone number. It treated the home city in a person's markup as a business address. It counted pages whose canonical tag names a different page as competing with that page. And one index page could pull a whole series into one "target the same search" group: a page for each of 29 states and their index counted as one search.
entries.found: We audited all seven of our own sites and read every finding against the live page. Five findings were Docket's mistake, not the site's.
entries.fixed: A day in an ISO or written date, a month and year, and a run of years are no longer an address or a phone number. A person's address no longer makes a local business. A page that names another as its canonical stops competing with it. A section index no longer glues its pages into one group, and Virginia and West Virginia are two places.
entries.result: On the same crawl before and after, the app site's score went from 89.9 to 92.3 and its four local findings went. A portfolio site went from 91.8 to 98.0. The series site's competing-pages finding fell from 53 pages in 6 groups to 13 in 6; the pairs left are calculators that share a title ending and two overlaps that look real.

entries.title: The link check looked at one host thirty times, and the topic step threw away its answers
entries.wrong: The outbound link check took the first 60 links in page order. On our own site 30 of its 61 targets were Buy and Download links to the same host, so the sample said little about the rest. Separately, the step that suggests topics asked a search engine's autocomplete for 18 commercial phrasings for each seed word and then discarded every answer. The stage between the link check and rendering took 30 to 34 seconds on the installed copy.
entries.found: Measuring the installed copy one stage at a time. With a counting wrapper on the same code, two seed words made 62 requests and spent 32.3 seconds in that step.
entries.fixed: The sample takes at most 8 links to any one site, and the report says "at most 8 to any one site" so it does not claim to have checked more. The topic step now asks only for the phrasings it keeps.
entries.result: Side by side against the live search engine, the same seeds made 62 calls in 38.3 seconds before and 26 calls in 13.0 seconds after, and the suggestions kept were identical in both pairs of runs (112 and 212). Dropping the commercial phrasings could in principle hide a later question behind an earlier completion; we did not see it in either pair.

entries.title: Outbound links waited in line behind the audited site's pace
entries.wrong: Every outbound link check went through the gap meant to protect the site being audited, so 60 requests to 60 other servers queued behind a pace of four a second. The stage took 16.8 seconds of a 101-second audit. On a site whose robots.txt asked for ten seconds between requests it would have taken 600 seconds for 60 one-off links, which is why the check had a time budget that left links unchecked.
entries.found: Measuring the installed copy one stage at a time.
entries.fixed: Each other host now gets its own clock and its own gap, so different hosts are checked side by side. The audited site's own links keep the polite gap. A link the clock had no time for is now left out of the results, not recorded as status 0, which the report would have called unreachable.
entries.result: Installed, the links stage took 11.0 and 10.4 seconds against 16.8, and the whole audit 96.9 and 96.7 against 101 to 105. It is not under 5 seconds because 30 of the 61 targets went to one host, which 1.3.106 addresses.

entries.title: A page that followed Docket's own advice was still flagged
entries.wrong: The finding about old image formats prints a picture element with a WebP source and the JPEG kept as the fallback. A four-page test site with exactly that markup still had all 16 of its images reported as old formats, because the check read each image's src, and in that markup the src is the fallback by design. Following the tool's advice did not clear the tool's finding.
entries.found: Writing the how-to guide for that finding, we audited a four-page test site with plain image tags and again with the picture markup. Plain tags reported 16 images, correctly. The picture markup also reported 16.
entries.fixed: An image in a picture element with a WebP or AVIF source, or with a srcset that names only such files, now counts as modern. A picture of JPEG sources, a mixed srcset and a plain image are still reported. JPEG XL is not counted: MDN, read on 10 October 2026, says its browser support is not yet universal.

see.text: The guide for that finding, which says the bug existed

entries.title: A franchise and a church: four findings that were false
entries.wrong: On a plumbing franchise with a section for each location, Docket said 309 pages in 69 groups targeted the same search. They were the same services in different towns, each location writing its own template around the place name. It also told that site that marking up its reviews of itself would earn stars in search, which Google's review-snippet guidelines (read 9 October 2026) rule out for a business reviewing itself. On a church site it said there was no LocalBusiness markup on a local business, gave it a LocalBusiness block to paste, and told it that it had no customer reviews.
entries.found: Two offline audits of real sites, each finding read against the pages. The rest of what Docket reported on both sites was true.
entries.fixed: A town, county or state named in a title now sets two pages apart, and a contact page no longer competes with a service page. Reviews count only on a page about a thing, such as a product, a recipe or an event. A place of worship is recognised from its name and is offered Church markup, and the no-reviews finding applies to businesses only.
entries.result: On the same crawl the franchise went from 309 pages in 69 groups to 13 in 6. The 13 include one town's service written twice, which do compete.

entries.title: Refresh said everything was up to date over rows that were a week old
entries.wrong: Refresh answered "Up to date: 4 sites, nothing changed" while every row on the watch list read "7d ago" on a daily schedule. The button compared the lengths of two lists. The scheduler runs only while the app is open and took one overdue site a minute, so a copy that had been closed for a week was minutes from current and said nothing.
entries.found: From a screenshot of the watch list.
entries.fixed: Refresh now checks every overdue site, one after another, and says how many it started. An overdue row says so, a check that failed shows its reason on its row, and the header says checks run while the app is open and catch up when it opens.
entries.unproven: We could not read the copy in the screenshot, so we do not know whether it had been closed or was failing. The new row text shows which.

entries.title: A text-message number was called not clickable, and a business with no shop was asked for an address
entries.wrong: A business that publishes its number only as sms: links, by design, was told the number was not clickable and to wrap it in tel: links, which invites calls the business does not take. A service-area business that declares where it serves was told to put a street address in its footer, the opposite of Google's guidance for such a business.
entries.found: Both showed up in the top five findings of the business in our own public sample report. Read against its live pages, the home page had six sms: links, no tel: link and a declared service area.
entries.fixed: sms: and smsto: links now count as click-to-contact, and where the finding still applies its fix offers an sms: link for a number that takes texts. A service-area business is no longer asked for an address. Both were tested in both directions: the real case is left alone and the same site without the sms: link, or without the service-area signal, is still reported.

entries.title: Tags added by JavaScript were reported as missing
entries.wrong: Docket told a games publisher that analytics was missing from 30 of 30 pages and that no other analytics ran anywhere. The site loads Tag Manager, GA4, Google Ads and the Meta pixel with JavaScript, so the served HTML had none of them and a browser had all of them. Two checks about JavaScript also flagged a framework's login page as invisible to AI crawlers and a password-reset page as very thin, though nobody searches for either.
entries.found: A sweep of well-built sites, with a deliberately defective control site that had to fire and did. Each high-severity finding was read against the live page. Most of the others were true: one browser maker's home page really does carry no structured data.
entries.fixed: When a render finds tags on a page whose served HTML showed none, the served-only gap is stood down. Login and password pages are skipped by both JavaScript checks. The release also fixed a case where a render cleared the flag on a page that is an empty single-page-app shell, which is still one word of content after rendering.
entries.unproven: One payments company's very-thin finding could not be rechecked that day, because the audit refused to run while a build was in progress. It was carried to the next round.
